Open the syntax reference · Read the textbook · Homework map

Lecture Focus Textbook connection
0 · Course overview Learn language concepts by defining a small language and implementing its interpreter. OCaml is the implementation tool; the interpreted language is a separate object of study. Chapter 1
1 · Inductive definitions I Define an infinite set using finite base and construction rules, with no extra elements. Chapter 1
2 · Inductive definitions II The shape of a datatype determines the cases of its recursive functions and structural proofs. Chapter 1
3 · Basics of OCaml Read OCaml as expressions built from bindings, functions, patterns, and typed values. Chapter 2
4 · Recursion and higher-order programming Solve a smaller instance, then combine its result; abstract repeated traversal with functions. Chapter 2
5 · Expressions and environments Translate each evaluation rule into a matching AST case and keep the environment explicit. Chapter 3
6 · Procedures and recursive closures A lexical procedure carries the environment where it was defined; a call extends that saved environment. Chapter 4
7 · Lexical addresses and nameless programs Resolve a variable to its binder statically and replace names with positions. Chapter 4
8 · State and parameter passing Separate the binding map from mutable memory and carry the updated store through every evaluation step. Chapter 6
9 · Records, pointers, and garbage collection Follow locations through structured values and distinguish unreachable memory from memory that merely looks unused. Chapter 7
10 · Exceptions and continuations Make pending computation explicit so a raised exception can discard frames up to the nearest handler. Dedicated slide topic
11 · Classes and objects An object combines mutable field locations with a class identity used for method lookup. Dedicated slide topic
12 · Why static types? Use a computable static approximation to prevent a specified class of runtime type errors. Chapter 8
13 · Designing typing rules Build typing derivations using a type environment instead of executing the program. Chapter 8
14 · Manual type annotations Explicit procedure annotations make syntax-directed checking possible without guessing parameter types. Chapter 8
15 · Type inference I: the idea Infer unknown types from how expressions are used, by turning typing rules into equations. Chapter 8
16 · Type inference II: constraint generation Define V(Γ,e,t) to generate the equalities required for expression e to have target type t. Chapter 8
17 · Type inference III: unification Solve type equations by substitution, decomposition, mismatch rejection, and the occurs check. Chapter 8
18 · Let-polymorphism Generalize independent type variables at let bindings and instantiate them freshly at each use. Chapter 8
19 · Typed objects and subtyping Check class programs using safe substitutability, with contravariant method inputs and covariant outputs. Dedicated slide topic
20 · Lambda calculus Understand functions and application as a small core, then make binding and reduction strategy precise. Chapter 9
